title: Cap. VII: Secunda responsio — 1 Cor. 15:22 and hereditary corruption neglected
pass_a_gloss: Second Garissoles reply: same fault of missing the argument; he also mishandles the so-called uncertain cause, and some of his wording is off. He asks how anyone can call Paul's cause uncertain when 1 Corinthians 15:22 climbs all the way to Adam the protoplast and declares that we all die in Adam. Placeus presses the relevance: does that verse supply a reason why all die by virtue of their communion with Adam? And must 'in Adam all die' be read even in the imputative sense of the opposing school? What comes next is worse. Garissoles claims that in neither passage does Paul attend to particular causes lodged in each human individual as the grounds of dying; he rather lays down a genus-wide cause that bears equally on all, etc. That talk treats hereditary corruption as if it were not already such a genus-wide cause — though it is no less shared than the death of sinners, than human nature itself, or than the imputation they promote. Step by step, then, the reformers' hard-won teaching on the force and guilt of hereditary corruption is set aside and almost erased, to clear space for an imputation those same great men either never taught or actively refuted.
pass_b_english: The second response likewise sins by ignorance of the argument, and takes the uncertain cause otherwise than it ought, and besides has some things less rightly said. "Who will have said," he says, "that an uncertain cause is proposed by Paul, when in 1 Corinthians 15:22 he ascends as far as Adam the first-formed, and says that we all die in Adam?" What is the point of this? Does the Apostle there bring forward some cause why all die by the force of the communion they have with Adam? Or are those words, "in Adam all die" (1 Corinthians 15:22), to be understood even imputatively, as they speak? Worse are the things that follow. "Namely," he says, "neither there nor here does the Apostle properly look to particular causes that can reside in each individual of the human race and on account of which it comes about that they die; but he sets out a general cause that looks upon all in the genus equally," and so on. He speaks just as if hereditary corruption were not a general cause looking upon all men equally — when yet that is as common as the death of those who have sinned is common, as human nature is common to them, indeed as imputation is said to be common. So little by little the doctrine of the force and guilt of hereditary corruption, which the first reformers defended with highest zeal, is neglected and nearly blotted out, that it may give place to that imputation which those great men either altogether did not know, or even refuted.
source_text: Secunda similiter responsio peccat ignoratione argumenti, causamque incertam aliter quam debuit accipit, et praeterea nonnulla habet minus recte dicta. Quis dixerit, inquit, incertam causam a Paulo proponi cum I. Cor. xv. 22. ad Adamum usque protoplastam conscendit, et nos omnes dicit in Adamo mori? Quorsum hoc spectat? Ibine causam aliquam affert Apostolus, cur omnes vi communionis quam habent cum Adamo moriantur? aut suntne illa verba, in Adamo omnes moriuntur, etiam imputative, ut loquuntur, intelligenda? Deteriora sunt quae sequuntur. Nimirum, inquit, neque ibi, neque hic Apostolus proprie ad causas particulares respicit, quae residere possunt in unoquoque individuo generis humani, et propter quas fit ut moriantur: sed causam generalem exponit quae omnes in genere ex aequo respiciat etc. Perinde loquitur, quasi corruptio haereditaria non esset causa generalis omnes homines ex aequo respiciens: Cum illa tamen tam sit communis, quam communis est eorum qui peccaverunt mors, quam communis est illis natura humana, immo quam communis dicitur esse imputatio. Ita paulatim doctrina de corruptionis haereditariae vi et reatu, quam summo studio primi reformatores tuebantur, negligitur ac prope obliteratur, ut det locum illi imputationi, quam magni illi viri, aut ignorarunt prorsus, aut etiam refutarunt.
